**Project Proposal: Cost-Aware AgentRouter**

**Course:** Summer 2026 CSC 504 & SENG 404

**Group Number:** 13

**Team Members:** Ziming Dong, Nhan Huynh, Ming Chen, Jason Thomo

# **1\. Project Motivation & Goal**

AI coding agents (Codex, Devin, Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) are now routinely opening pull requests on public GitHub. Published AIDev follow-ups have analyzed their security, test contributions, code survival, and review themes, but none treat agent identity as a decision variable. Yet the agents differ by an order of magnitude in subscription cost, so which one a team picks for a given task matters in dollars, not only in PR merge rate.

We propose a **two-stage cost-aware routing framework** that dispatches a GitHub issue to one of the five agents above. Stage 1 — the router — predicts merge probability per agent from issue features and selects the agent that maximises a cost-adjusted utility (Section 5, Eq. 1); Stage 2 triages the resulting pull request, predicting whether it will merge cleanly, merge after revision, or be closed. The deliverable is an offline empirical study: a trained router, a held-out evaluation against random and always-best-agent baselines, and an interpretable feature-importance analysis explaining when each agent wins.

# **2\. Related Work**

*Empirical studies on AI coding agents.* The release of the AIDev dataset has motivated a wave of empirical work analyzing agentic pull requests along specific quality dimensions: security vulnerabilities introduced by agents \[Security in the Age of AI Teammates\], the prevalence and adequacy of agent-contributed tests \[Do Autonomous Agents Contribute Test Code?\], the long-term survival of AI-generated code in open-source projects \[Will It Survive?\], and the dominant themes in how human reviewers respond to agentic PRs \[Understanding Dominant Themes\]. The original AIDev paper \[Li et al., 2026\] and the broader SE 3.0 vision \[Li et al., 2025\] frame these agents as first-class collaborators in the software process. A methodologically adjacent line of work uses per-commit and per-PR classifiers to predict merge or defect outcomes \[Ni et al., 2024 on JIT defect prediction\], but does so without modeling who authored the change. Collectively, these works characterize *what agents do* and *how well they do it*, but they treat agent identity as a descriptive variable rather than a decision variable — they do not ask whether the choice of agent itself could have been made better.

*LLM and agent routing.* In parallel, a separate line of work has studied cost-aware routing among general-purpose LLMs. RouteLLM \[Ong et al., 2025\] learns a binary router between a strong and a weak model from preference data; Hybrid LLM \[Ding et al., 2024\] casts the same problem as quality-aware query routing; FrugalGPT \[Chen et al., 2024\] cascades models to reduce inference cost while preserving accuracy. These methods consistently show that learned routing dominates the “always use the strongest model” baseline on the cost-quality Pareto front, but they are evaluated on short-form QA, summarization, and reasoning benchmarks — not on long-horizon software engineering tasks such as resolving GitHub issues.

*Our position.* Our work sits at the intersection of these two threads. We adopt RouteLLM's formulation — a learned router over query features that selects among candidates to maximize a utility net of cost — and re-target it to *agent selection* at the GitHub-issue level, using merge outcome as a real-world proxy for task success rather than the synthetic benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench \[Jimenez et al., 2024\]) used elsewhere. No prior work, to our knowledge, frames AI coding agent selection as a learnable, cost-aware routing problem on real GitHub data.

# **3\. Research Questions**

- **RQ1.** Do the five agents (Codex, Devin, Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code) show measurably different merge rates across task categories such as repo language, issue length, and the presence of code blocks or stack traces? *The primary confirmatory test is two-proportion z-tests across language × agent cells (Bonferroni-corrected); the other axes are examined descriptively.*

- **RQ2.** Given an unmerged issue, how accurately can a regressor predict per-agent success from task and repository features alone? *Reported as Stage 1 MAE against a per-agent-mean baseline.*

- **RQ3.** Does a learned router beat both "always pick the historically best agent" and "random agent" baselines on a held-out, repo-grouped test set, *evaluated within the observed (issue, agent) distribution*? Because each PR is authored by exactly one agent, we never observe the counterfactual outcome of an unused agent on the same issue; the router is scored against the realized agent assignment, not against a per-issue oracle. *Reported as routing success lift and mean cost on the held-out estimator.*

- **RQ4.** Does the cost-adjusted router dominate the success-only router on the cost-quality Pareto curve as λ varies? *Reported as (success rate, mean cost) pairs across λ ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10}.* *(Revised in the interim report: because Copilot is the only agent cheaper than Codex, the λ sweep reduces in practice to a Codex→Copilot budget sweep.)*

# **4\. Data Sources & Pilot Experiments**

We use AIDev. Rather than the smaller AIDev-pop subset, which holds too few minority-agent PRs to train a five-agent router (Claude Code and Cursor are especially thin there), we build a balanced corpus from the full \~932k-PR dump by down-sampling each agent to the smallest agent's count, yielding **\~25,580 PRs (\~5,116 per agent)**.

**Data Exploration.** We loaded the `all_pull_request` table into pandas and confirmed access to the columns we will rely on: *id, number, user\_id, state, created\_at, closed\_at, merged\_at, repo\_id, title, body, agent*. A 100-row sample (Figure 1) confirms the schema and access pattern; a stratified sample across all five agents, with per-agent merge rates, will replace this in the final report.

**Preprocessing.** We will encode `title` and `body` as feature vectors using TF-IDF as a baseline and a sentence-embedding model (e.g., `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`) as the second representation, then compare both on the validation set.

**Handling Imbalance.** Some agents and task types dominate the dataset. We balance the corpus by **down-sampling each agent to the smallest agent's count**, which preserves each agent's natural outcome distribution — the signal the router relies on. We evaluate the regressor with **MAE against a per-agent-mean baseline** and report results broken down by support size, not aggregated into a single number.

# **5\. Research Strategies & Workflow**

The system operates in two stages:

- **Stage 1 (Router).** An XGBoost regressor over task-level features predicts each agent's success (a continuous target: merged = 1.0, still-open = 0.3, closed-unmerged = 0.0). Because issue text is not available at routing time, the task proxy is the agent-authored PR `title` (a reduced-leakage signal), encoded with TF-IDF / a sentence-embedding model, alongside repository metadata (primary language, log stars, log forks), an issue-link flag, and a rule-derived task type. The router selects the agent maximising the utility:

  *utility(agent) = P(merge | issue, agent) − λ · cost(agent)*  *(Eq. 1)*

- **Stage 2 (PR Triage).** Once a PR exists, a secondary classifier uses PR-level features (diff size, description text, agent identity) to predict one of three outcomes: "clean merge," "merge after revision," or "closed without merge." Labels are derived from `state`, `merged_at`, and post-creation edits in the AIDev metadata. *(Revised in the interim report: this post-hoc triage stage was not pursued — it runs after a PR exists and so cannot inform the routing decision — and the related quality question is instead addressed by a descriptive review-friction analysis.)*

- **Cost model.** `cost(agent)` is a normalized **marginal per-PR price** in USD. Because the agents bill on different bases (token API, request/credit, ACU, backend-model pool), we convert each vendor's public pricing to a per-PR scenario: token-priced agents are sized by an agentic-PR token budget, and the rest are mapped to an approximate per-PR cost. The resulting scenario ranges from $1.10 (Copilot) to $4.80 (Claude Code), with Codex and Cursor at $3.85 and Devin at $4.50. We report results at two pricing snapshots (2024-Q4 and 2026-Q2) as a sensitivity check.

- **Splits.** We split by `repo_id` (70/15/15 train/val/test) to prevent within-repo leakage. *(A temporal hold-out of the most recent calendar month is planned as a generalisation check; see the interim report's future-work list.)*

- **Counterfactual handling.** AIDev records a single observed agent per PR, so there is no per-issue counterfactual: we cannot observe how an unused agent would have performed on the same issue (in practice only a handful of issues are attempted by two or more distinct agents). We therefore train Stage 1 as a per-agent success predictor on the observed (issue, agent) pairs and evaluate the router with a subgroup direct-method estimator — per-(language × task_type) cell success scored on held-out data — to value each policy's choices. This yields a within-distribution estimate of routing benefit, not a causal or counterfactual guarantee; establishing the latter would require randomized agent assignment or an explicit causal design, both out of scope here.

- **Pareto evaluation.** We sweep λ ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10} and report (success rate, mean cost) pairs on the held-out test set alongside the "always-best-agent" and "random-agent" baselines. Primary metrics are MAE (prediction quality), routing success at matched cost, and cost-adjusted utility from Eq. 1.

*Buffer:* the last three days before submission are reserved for re-running the pipeline end-to-end against the locked-down splits and final figure regeneration; no new modelling work is planned in that window.

**Tools & Compute.** Our core stack is Python (Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, XGBoost) for data processing and classical modeling, together with the Hugging Face datasets and transformers libraries for accessing AIDev and loading pretrained encoders.

For text features on the issue title and body, we plan to start with two complementary representations: (i) a TF-IDF baseline (uni- and bi-grams, with light preprocessing — lowercasing, code-fence stripping, URL/email normalization) to give us an interpretable and cheap reference point, and (ii) dense embeddings from a sentence-embedding or code-aware encoder (e.g., a MiniLM/MPNet sentence model or a code-search encoder), better suited to the mixed natural-language-and-code text found in GitHub issues than a purely NL baseline. These will be concatenated with structured metadata features (e.g., repo primary language, repo size, issue length, presence of code blocks or stack traces, agent identity as a one-hot indicator) before being fed to the Stage 1 Router. This feature design is preliminary: depending on what we observe from ablations in Week 2, we may

- swap in a larger or more recent encoder (e.g., bge-code, e5-code, or a CodeT5+ encoder);
- add LLM-generated summaries of long issues as an auxiliary feature; or
- fall back to TF-IDF alone if dense embeddings do not yield a meaningful MAE improvement over the cost of computing them.

For compute, we have a local workstation with an RTX 5090 (sufficient for embedding extraction over the \~25,580-PR corpus and for all XGBoost training), and we additionally have access to Compute Canada for larger sweeps and any encoder fine-tuning we may decide to run. We do not anticipate API costs, since all proposed models can be served locally. We are aware of the need for robust validation to avoid overfitting, and will use repo-level group splits to prevent leakage between train and test.

# **7\. Potential Limitations**

- **Selection Bias & Missing Counterfactual.** Agents were chosen by humans, not randomly assigned, so the data reflects existing habits rather than each agent’s true capability. Critically, each PR is authored by exactly one agent, so we never observe how a different agent would have fared on the same issue — there is no per-issue counterfactual. Our router is therefore trained and scored on the realized (issue, agent) assignment; it predicts within this observed distribution and we make no claim of causal or counterfactual optimality. Establishing the latter would require randomized agent assignment or an explicit causal-inference design, both out of scope for this offline study.

- **Proxy Metrics.** Merge status is a noisy signal for quality (a closed PR isn’t always a “failure”), and our cost estimate covers API/subscription price but not human review time. We will state our definitions explicitly and check that conclusions don’t hinge on a single choice.

- **Data Imbalance.** Some agents and languages dominate the dataset. We mitigate this by down-sampling each agent to the smallest agent's count and by reporting MAE with per-cell results by support size, rather than a single aggregate number. Note that balancing trades against the per-agent base rate, which is itself part of the routing signal.

- **Distribution Shift.** The agents themselves keep changing (Copilot in 2024 ≠ Copilot in 2026), so a router trained on AIDev is best viewed as a feasibility study, not a deployment-ready system.

- **External Validity.** AIDev covers public OSS PRs only; results may not transfer to enterprise codebases or under-represented languages.

- **Cost-model validity.** Vendor pricing is a noisy proxy for marginal compute. Subscription prices changed multiple times during AIDev's observation window; we report results at two pricing snapshots (2024-Q4 and 2026-Q2) as a sensitivity check rather than committing to a single number.

# **8\. Expected Results**

1. **Per-agent variation (RQ1).** Different agents show statistically significant merge-rate gaps across task categories (repo language, issue length, presence of stack traces), tested by two-proportion z-tests with Bonferroni correction across language × agent cells. This validates the premise of routing.

2. **Router lift (RQ3, RQ4) — hypothesis.** We hypothesise that a cost-aware router improves cost-adjusted utility (Eq. 1) over both the "always-best-agent" and "random-agent" baselines on the held-out, repo-grouped test set. We frame any such lift as a *within-distribution* result: because the data contains a single observed agent per PR, it measures improvement over the realized assignment policy, not a counterfactual guarantee that the router's chosen agent would have merged had it actually been used. *(Revised in the interim report: on success alone no learned router beats always-best-agent — that baseline turns out to be strong and selection-bias-driven — and the router's value is confined to the cost axis, where a cell cost-gap router keeps ~93% of always-best success at ~29% lower cost.)*

3. **Interpretable signals.** SHAP feature importances on the Stage 1 Router surface a small set of issue-level signals (issue length, code-block presence, language tag, stack-trace presence) that explain *why* a given agent wins on a given task. We view this as the main practical contribution beyond raw routing accuracy. *(Revised in the interim report: interpretability is instead reported via feature-ablations showing the task text contributes little over agent identity and repository metadata; a formal SHAP analysis remains future work.)*
